exit_trigger: Evidence that customers are switching suppliers or that pricing power has eroded, such as sustained margin compression; Sustained decline of ROE well below 15% without a clear temporary cause; Debt-to-equity rising materially above 0.5 or leverage-funded buybacks at high prices; Management dishonesty, restatements, or value-destroying acquisitions; Price above 1.5x a conservatively re-derived intrinsic value, with the gap persisting
rationale: I own this one, and I own it at a loss: 1 share bought at $886.815 on 2026-08-07, now $695.02, down 21.63%. A lower price on a business whose economics haven't changed is not a reason to sell; it is the reason I'd add if the numbers hold up. The snapshot shows a five-year average ROE of 30.6%, debt-to-equity of 0.4968 (just inside my 0.5 limit), and average owner earnings of about $413 million against a $6.5 billion market cap. The model's $1,271.73 value and 45% margin of safety lean on 8% growth against a 5% discount rate, which is generous, so I haircut it and won't add on that figure alone. I keep the position and keep watching the moat, because the margin of safety only matters if the moat is real.

rationale: I own this one, down about 15.85% from my $128.38 entry 96 days ago, and a price drop alone is no reason to sell if the brand is intact. But the model's $346.97 intrinsic value leans on 8% growth for a decade at a 5% discount rate, and I would not bet the farm on that. Athletic apparel also sits uncomfortably near the fashion-driven businesses I avoid, and the snapshot does not show 10 years of earnings, CEO tenure or ROIC, so I cannot confirm those criteria. I keep the shares, I do not add until I can verify the brand's pricing power, and I will sell if the moat erodes, not because the quote fell.

exit_trigger: Evidence that franchise-law protection is weakening or manufacturers move to direct-to-consumer sales at scale; Service and parts profits declining materially, showing the stable earnings base is eroding; Return on equity falling persistently below 15% or debt-to-equity rising above 0.5; Management making value-destroying acquisitions or buybacks at peak prices, or losing candor with shareholders; Price exceeding 1.5x intrinsic value with the gap persisting
rationale: I own this one, a small position of 6 shares bought at $216.765 and now down about 1.85%, and the question is whether to keep it. The numbers I can see are decent: a 5-year average ROE of 23.8%, debt-to-equity of 0.39, and a price of $212.75 against a model value of $259.62, an 18.05% margin of safety on a no-growth assumption. But a car dealer is a tough business, and the moat here is thin, mostly franchise-law protection and local scale rather than a brand that lets you raise prices every year. Nothing in this snapshot tells me about ten years of earnings consistency, management tenure or capital allocation, so I cannot call this a wonderful company, and I keep my confidence low. I'll keep what I have, I won't add until I can verify those gaps, and I'll sell if the moat proves weaker than I think.

rationale: I own 11 shares of MSM, bought 16 days ago at $120.05, and the position is up 0.87%, which tells me nothing except that I haven't yet been wrong. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 20.03%, debt-to-equity of 0.35, and owner earnings averaging about $303 million, against a market cap of about $6.76 billion. My estimate of intrinsic value is $157.18 a share, a 22.95% margin of safety, which clears my 15% bar. I'm keeping it, not adding yet. The snapshot says nothing about the 10-year earnings record, ROIC, or CEO tenure, so my conviction stays moderate, and the valuation rests on a 5% discount rate and 8% growth that I would treat with caution. A distributor's moat is scale and service, not a Coca-Cola brand, and I'll watch it closely.

exit_trigger: Evidence of brand or channel pricing-power erosion, such as sustained margin compression; Management making large value-destroying acquisitions or abandoning capital discipline; Price exceeding 1.5x intrinsic value with the gap persisting; Material technological shift that undermines the core product category
rationale: I own this one, 21 shares bought at $61.505 nineteen days ago, and I'm sitting on a 4.41% gain that tells me nothing about the business. What I can see in the snapshot is a company earning a 5-year average ROE of 23.66% with debt-to-equity of just 0.083, and a price of $64.22 against a conservative owner-earnings estimate of $95.72 a share, roughly a 33% margin of safety. The snapshot does not give me ten years of earnings history, the CEO's tenure, or the competitive-share data that would prove the moat, so I hold what I have and do not press it harder until I can check those. Time is the friend of the wonderful business; I'll let it work and not fidget over a few weeks of price.

exit_trigger: Evidence of brand pricing power eroding, such as sustained volume loss after price increases or share loss to private label; Management destroying value through large acquisitions at poor prices or dishonest reporting; Price persistently above 1.5x intrinsic value with no growth in owner earnings; Filings showing debt materially higher than the snapshot's debt-to-equity implies, undermining the balance sheet case
rationale: I own this one, and the question today is whether anything has changed since we bought it thirteen days ago. Nothing has. I understand a business that sells paint, sealants and coatings people reach for by name, and the snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 22.9% and a margin of safety of 21.2% against my 15% minimum. What keeps me from pounding the table is what I cannot verify here: the debt-to-equity of 0.0027 looks too tidy to trust without seeing the filing, and the owner earnings yield on the current market cap is only about 4.4%, which is thin next to the discount rate of 5% in the snapshot. The 10-year earnings record, CEO tenure and insider activity are also not in the data. So I keep the position at its current size, add nothing until those gaps close, and let time work. A small gain after thirteen days tells me nothing, and I don't sell on price noise.

exit_trigger: Evidence of eroding pricing power or declining service and installed-base retention; Management destroying value through large acquisitions at peak prices; Technological shifts that commoditize its automation offering; Price above 1.5x a conservatively verified intrinsic value
rationale: I don't own Emerson, and this is the buy-or-wait question. On the numbers in front of me it looks like a good business: 5-year average ROE of 30.6%, debt-to-equity of 0.44, and a market cap near $94.8 billion. The model shows a 38% margin of safety, but that rests on an 8% growth assumption and a 5% discount rate, and I would haircut it before trusting it. Owner earnings of about $5.3 billion against that market cap is roughly a 5.6% yield, which is not a bargain. I also can't see ten years of earnings history, CEO tenure, or the Treasury yield for my yield test, and the book already holds ten names. When the checklist isn't complete I wait. I'll sit on my hands until I can verify the earnings record and the management record.

exit_trigger: Evidence that the cost and scale advantage is eroding, for example from imports or substitute materials such as plastic piping taking durable share; Margins and ROE sliding toward ordinary industrial levels on a sustained basis; Management making value-destroying acquisitions or buybacks at inflated prices, or any accounting irregularity; Price exceeding 1.5x a verified, conservatively normalized intrinsic value with the gap persisting; A far better opportunity of much higher conviction that requires the capital
rationale: I own this one, and the question is whether to keep it, not whether to open it. I understand a metals fabricator that turns copper into pipe and fittings. It is the kind of commodity-adjacent business I normally treat with suspicion, because the moat has to come from scale and cost position, not pricing power. The numbers in front of me are strong: a 5-year average ROE of 29.3%, debt-to-equity reported at 0.0, and average owner earnings of about $646 million against a $6.1 billion market cap. But the model's $168.53 intrinsic value is three times the price, and when a spreadsheet says that, I trust the spreadsheet less, not the stock more. Those owner earnings may be flattered by a cyclical peak, and the snapshot lacks the 10-year earnings record and the ROIC to settle it. Nothing here breaks the thesis after six days, so I keep the shares, add nothing until I can verify the durability, and sell only if the cost advantage erodes.
